html:
An Indian law passed in August 2005 that gave every rural household a legal right to up to 100 days of paid manual work a year on public works, at a set minimum wage.

It was passed under the government of Manmohan Singh, drawing on Maharashtra's own job scheme of the 1970s and on campaigns by activists and economists such as Jean Drèze. It started in February 2006 in the poorest districts and covered the whole country by 2008. In 2009 it was named after Mahatma Gandhi. Work was to be given within 15 days of asking, close to home, mostly digging ponds, building roads and conserving soil and water.

It became one of the largest public works programmes in the world, reaching tens of millions of households each year. Women did about half the work, often their first paid jobs. Critics pointed to delays in wages, corruption and the quality of the assets built; supporters pointed to higher rural wages and a safety net in droughts. During Covid, when migrants returned to their villages, demand reached record levels. In December 2025 Parliament passed a law to replace it with a new rural jobs scheme.
sum: An Indian law passed in August 2005 that gave every rural household a legal right to up to 100 days of paid manual work a year on public works, at a set minimum wage.
